Those two arcs on this map are why 13 days in October 1962 felt like the closest the world has come to nuclear war.

a thread 🧵🗺️
1/ The crisis ran from 16 to 28 October 1962. The Soviets were building nine missile sites in Cuba: six for R-12 missiles and three for the longer-range R-14.
2/ The R-12, a medium-range missile, had an effective range of about 2,000 km. That's the inner dashed arc on the map, enough to reach a big part of the southeastern US.
3/ The R-14, an intermediate-range missile, could travel up to about 4,500 km. That's the outer arc, putting almost every major US city in range, except part of the northwest.
4/ Unknown to the US at the time, 162 Soviet nuclear warheads were already on Cuba. That one fact makes the crisis even more dangerous than it looked from Washington.
5/ On 27 October, a US Navy ship dropped signalling depth charges near the Soviet submarine B-59, armed with a nuclear torpedo. Flotilla commander Vasily Arkhipov refused to approve a launch.
6/ It ended with a public deal: Soviet missiles out of Cuba, a US pledge not to invade. Secretly, the US also agreed to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey, which became public later.
7/ Did the world get lucky in 1962? Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
